catalog_quote: Every word has one syllable with a primary stress, and usually one or more unstressed syllables. In words of two or more syllables, the syllable containing the second vowel is stressed. Thus the first syllable is stressed if it contains a geminate vowel (46a) or a diphthong (46b). In all the other cases the second syllable is stressed (46c). When the stressed syllable is long, the stress falls equally on the whole vowel sequence (46d–e). (46) a. /aasa/ [ˈaː.sa] ‘canoe’ b. /kuija/ [ˈkui.ja] ‘it bites’ c. /aɸura/ [a.ˈɸu.ra] ‘lime’ d. /siowa/ [si.ˈo.wa] ‘dog’ e. /isaimija/ [i.ˈsai.mi.ja] ‘(s)he heats (food)’ Both derivational and inflectional affixes may receive primary stress provided they are in a position where stress is normally placed (47) ... audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated page (book p. 42 / PDF p. 58, sec. 2.3.1; domain quote p. 34 / PDF p. 50). The deciding source is a modern 516-page open-access reference grammar by the long-term fieldworker, the top item in Glottolog's descriptive bibliography; every other descriptive reference is by the same two SIL authors and either unpublished (1980, 1989 mss) or the 2010 thesis that the 2015 book supersedes. The coding (kind=weight, left edge, CVV heavy: stress on the syllable containing the second vowel, i.e. initial if geminate vowel/diphthong else second syllable; affixes count, clitics do not; secondary stress in compounds/reduplication) matches the source text exactly, and the grammar calls the rule 'otherwise exceptionless'. No better source exists to change it; only a low-priority wish for the author's 1989 unpublished phonology ms.
